title: The Harmonic Series
intro: A plucked string or a blown pipe vibrates at its fundamental frequency and at every whole-number multiple of it at once. These partials, the harmonic series, give a tone its colour, and the simplest intervals of music appear in it as ratios of small whole numbers.

blocks.text: A string fixed at both ends can only vibrate in patterns that fit a whole number of half-waves between the ends. The longest pattern is the fundamental, frequency $f_0$. The next fits two half-waves, so its wavelength is half as long and its frequency $2f_0$; then $3f_0$, $4f_0$ and so on. A real string vibrates in all these modes at once. Air columns in flutes, clarinets and brass behave the same way (a clarinet's closed tube favours the odd harmonics).

widget.title: The partials of a harmonic tone

blocks.text: The partials are evenly spaced in hertz, but the ear hears pitch logarithmically, so they crowd together as they go up. A larger roll-off exponent makes a darker, mellower tone (flute-like); a small one makes a bright, buzzy tone (like a sawtooth or a bowed string).
Starting on C2 (65.4 Hz), the first sixteen harmonics are, approximately:

items: 1: C2 (fundamental) · 2: C3 (octave) · 3: G3 (octave + fifth) · 4: C4 (two octaves)
5: E4 (major third above C4, 14 cents flat of equal temperament) · 6: G4 · 7: B♭4 (31 cents flat) · 8: C5
9: D5 (4 cents sharp) · 10: E5 · 11: between F5 and F♯5 (49 cents flat of F♯) · 12: G5
13: between G♯5 and A5 (41 cents sharp of G♯, 59 cents flat of A) · 14: B♭5 · 15: B5 · 16: C6

blocks.text: Read off neighbouring harmonics and the intervals of music appear as small ratios: 2:1 is the octave, 3:2 the perfect fifth, 4:3 the perfect fourth, 5:4 the major third, 6:5 the minor third. Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 together make a major triad, C–E–G, with frequency ratios 4:5:6.

When two tones are a simple ratio apart, many of their partials coincide. For a fifth (3:2), every second partial of the upper tone lands exactly on every third partial of the lower one. Partials that nearly coincide but not quite produce beating and roughness, which the ear hears as dissonance. The Consonance and Dissonance (#/arts/music-theory/intervals/consonance) page plots this effect.

Two tones in a simple ratio also add up to a waveform that repeats quickly. The plot below sums the three notes of a chord. A just major triad (4:5:6) repeats every four periods of its root; the equal-tempered triad drifts and never quite repeats.

Overtone is an older word for a partial above the fundamental, counted from 1: the first overtone is the second harmonic. Partial counts the fundamental as partial 1, so for a harmonic tone partial k is harmonic k. Bells, drums and xylophone bars are not strings: their partials are not whole-number multiples (they are inharmonic), which is why a bell's pitch can sound ambiguous.

blocks.title: Find the harmonic
blocks.text: Which harmonic of A2 (110 Hz) is closest to E5?
solution: E5 is about 659.3 Hz. 659.3 / 110 ≈ 5.99, so it is the 6th harmonic, 660 Hz, which is a pure (3:2) fifth above A4 and 2 cents above equal-tempered E5.

blocks.title: Coinciding partials
blocks.text: For two tones a perfect fourth (4:3) apart, which partials of each coincide?
solution: The lower tone has partials at f, 2f, 3f, 4f, …; the upper at (4/3)f, (8/3)f, 4f, … The upper tone's 3rd partial equals the lower tone's 4th (both 4f), and every multiple of those: upper 6 = lower 8, upper 9 = lower 12, and so on.

blocks.title: The seventh harmonic
blocks.text: Harmonic 7 of C2 is called a 'flat' B♭. How many cents is 7/4 from the equal-tempered minor seventh (1000 cents)?
solution: 1200 × log2(7/4) = 1200 × 0.80735 ≈ 968.8 cents, so it is about 31 cents flatter than the equal-tempered B♭.
